application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In this paper we present a novel approach to the constrained scheduling problem, while addressing a more general class of constraints that arise from the timing requirements on real-time embedded controllers and from the implementation of mixed data-flow/event-driven real-time systems. We provide general necessary and sufficient conditions for scheduling under precedence constraints and derive sufficient conditions for two well-known scheduling policies. We define mathematical problems that provide optimum priority and deadline assignments, while ensuring both precedence constraints and system's schedulability. We show how these problems can be relaxed to corresponding ILP formulations leveraging on available solvers.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The design of real-time systems is usually approached by decomposing the system in a set of tasks that are scheduled on a set of processing resources. Real-time requirements impose constraints on the necessary computational resources. For these reasons, the scientific community has focused on establishing the conditions by which the task set is schedulable on a set of processing resources by some scheduling policy under given real-time requirements.

For fixed priority (FP) scheduling on uniprocessor it has been shown [10,8] that, under certain conditions, the system's schedulability is maximized when the priorities are chosen in the inverse order of the tasks' deadlines (deadline monotonic scheduling). A similar condition has also been shown [10] for dynamic scheduling on uniprocessor, where under certain conditions schedulability is maximized when higher priorities are given to the tasks with lower absolute deadlines. This scheduling policy is known as the earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduling policy. An alternative well-known scheduling policy with dynamic priorities which maximize schedulability is represented by the least laxity first (LLF) policy, which however introduces more task preemptions than the EDF policy.

Additional constraints on the software implementation of real-time systems arise when deterministic communication between tasks is required [13], which introduces precedence constraints on tasks executions: if task τ i is the producer of the communication data and τ j is the consumer, then the execution of τ i must precede the execution of τ j . In the traditional concept of precedence constraints, the tasks involved are required to have the same period. In this paper we extend the notion of precedence to allow for constraints between tasks with different periods, which has applications in embedded systems design.

Precedence constraints may affect the system's schedulability. Indeed, it is well-known that precedence constraints in real-time scheduling problems can be guaranteed by priority assignment. For example, in fixed priority scheduling any task τ i will always precede any lower priority task τ j , provided that τ i is not released later than τ j . Similarly, with EDF any task will always precede any other task with later deadline. This fact suggests the following immediate result: we say that a precedence constraint that requires τ i to precede τ j is "consistent" with their deadlines if τ i has earlier deadline than τ j . Then, precedence constraints that are consistent with the tasks' deadlines do not affect the uniprocessor schedulability of the task set. In fact, by using the deadline monotonic assignment for fixed priority scheduling or the EDF scheduling policy, uniprocessor schedulability is maximized and the precedence constraints are satisfied.

A different situation arises when the precedence constraints are not all consistent with the tasks' deadlines. In such a case the system's schedulability is affected, i.e. the task set might be non-schedulable under precedence constraints, while being schedulable without precedence constraints. We will show in this paper that in such cases schedulability may be recovered by considering a constrained scheduling problem based on a more general class of precedence constraints, that can be "relaxed" to account for schedulability.

div.head: Previous work
div.p: The scheduling problem under precedence constraints arise from several applications. A classical problem consists in scheduling a set of parallel activities on a given number of processing resources. Since these parallel activities represent a global computation they may be subjected to precedence constraints. The resulting constrained scheduling problem consists in finding an optimum schedule of a finite number of jobs on given processing units. This problem has been formalized as an ILP problem by several authors for both uniprocessor [7] and multiprocessors [11,6].

A distinct problem arises from real-time scheduling with deterministic communications. Communication constraints between tasks can be formulated as precedence constraints. In [13], the authors provide sufficient conditions for schedules to obey a given precedence graph 1 . Since they require that the precedence constraints be consistent with the task deadlines, in their case schedulability is not affected by the precedence constraints.
The main contributions of this paper to the scheduling problem under precedence constraints are the following:
• Generalized concept of scheduling constraints • Necessary and sufficient conditions for scheduling under precedence constraints in the general case
• Sufficient conditions for FP and EDF policies
• Formalization of the problems of optimum priority/deadline assignment for FP/EDF scheduling under precedence and schedulability constraints
• ILP relaxation of the optimization problems.

The paper is organized as follows: in Section 3 the scheduling problem under precedence constraints is introduced and generalized, while in Section 4 practical applications of the generalized problem are presented. Necessary and sufficient conditions for constrained scheduling for the general case are derived in Section 5. In Section 6, these general conditions are applied to specific scheduling policies to derive specific sufficient conditions. These conditions are used in Section 7 to formalize optimization problems of scheduling under precedence and schedulability constraints. Corresponding ILP formulations are provided in Section 8. Finally, conclusions are drawn in Section 9.

1 The authors claim that their Theorem 3.1 is a necessary and sufficient condition. A counter example shows that the condition is only sufficient: consider a task set comprising three tasks τ 1 , τ 2 and τ 3 with deadlines d 1 < d 2 < d 3 and release times r 1 ≤ r 2 ≤ r 3 . Assume that τ 1 must precede τ 2 , then the release times and deadlines are consistent with the partial order, and the schedule "τ 1 followed by τ 3 followed by τ 2 " obeys the partial order, but it is not quasi-normal (see [13] for details).

div.head: Task model and problem's definition
div.p: Our model is composed of a set of tasks τ i . Each task consists of a virtually infinite sequence of jobs that will be denoted by τ i (h). Every job is characterized by the following quantities, shown in Fig. 1: an arrival time a i (h), which denotes the time of the job's scheduling request, a release time r i (h), denoting the time at which the job is put on the ready queue, a start time s i (h) and a completion time f i (h), which denote the times at which the job starts and ends its execution. These quantities are characterized by the rela-
div.formula: tions a i (h) ≤ r i (h) ≤ s i (h) ≤ f i (h).
div.p: In the sequel we say that any job τ i (h) precedes a job τ j (k) if τ j (k) cannot start until τ i (h) has finished. This precedence relation is formalized as follows.

div.head: Def. 3.1 τ
div.formula: i (h) precedes τ j (k), denoted by τ i (h) ≺ τ j (k), if f i (h) ≤ s j (k).
div.p: In our model precedence constraints are defined by a directed graph, G, called the precedence graph, where each node represents a task and each directed arc represents a precedence constraint between two tasks. We represent the precedence graph by binary quantities, G i,j , such that G i,j = 1 if there is an arc in G from node i to node j, while G i,j = 0 otherwise.

In the literature the meaning of a precedence constraint is usually given as follows: G i,j = 1 ⇒ τ i (h) ≺ τ j (h), i.e. τ i precedes τ j if each job of τ i precedes a corresponding job of τ j . This definition is applicable in practice only to tasks that have the same rate. As it will be exemplified in Section 4, in many embedded systems applications the constrained scheduling problem must be defined in a more general case, where tasks may have different rates. In such a case the desired relation between the jobs of the two tasks is not a one-to-one relation as usually considered in the literature. Rather, it is determined by the arrival times of the jobs. We take this into account by conditioning the precedence constraints with the jobs' arrival order, which can be formalized as follows: G i,j = 1 and a i (h) ≤ a j (k) ⇒ τ i (h) ≺ τ j (k). Note that two indexes h and k are required
div.formula: a i (h) ≤ a j (k) ⇒ τ i (h) ≺ τ j (k + 2)
div.p: to express this more general relation, because the relation between jobs that we need to express is not one-to-one.

In this paper we introduce a further generalization of the traditional idea of precedence constraint. Let two nonnegative integers, d i,j and e i,j , be given for every arc in the precedence graph. The meaning that we attach to the precedence constraint is formalized in the following definition.

div.head: Def. 3.2 Any schedule is consistent with the precedence graph if G
div.formula: i,j = 1 and a i (h) ≤ a j (k) ⇒ τ i (h -d i,j ) ≺ τ j (k + e i,j )
div.p: The non-negative integers d i,j and e i,j represent a "relaxation" of the precedence constraint, in the sense that they impose looser requirements on the processing resources to schedule the tasks. For example in Fig. 2 it is shown that, although τ i (h) does not precede τ j (k), τ i (h) does precede τ j (k + 2).
Note that if τ i and τ j have the same rate and d i,j = e i,j = 0, we obtain the usual definition of precedence constraint.

The constrained scheduling problem can be defined as finding the conditions under which every schedule produced by a given scheduling policy is consistent with the precedence graph in the sense of Def. 3.2. For a given scheduling policy, such as FP or EDF, the problem can be reduced to finding a specific assignment to its parameters, e.g. priorities for FP and relative deadlines for EDF, that ensures consistency of any schedule with the precedence graph.

div.head: Motivations
div.p: In the present section we discuss two practical applications of the problem defined in Section 3.

Uniprocessor deterministic implementations of mixed data-flow/event-driven real-time systems: event-driven real-time systems are usually characterized by strict latency constraints, while data-flow computation is mainly characterized by rate constraints. Hence, mixed data-flow/event-driven real-time systems are best
div.formula: a i (h) ≤ a j (k) ⇒ τ i (h) ≺ τ j (k + 1)
div.p: schedulable when event-driven tasks have higher priority than data-flow tasks. Since event-driven tasks may execute several times before data-flow tasks complete a single execution, data queues must be implemented between these components in order not to lose relevant data.

For a given priority or deadline assignment to tasks it is not difficult to obtain finite bounds for these queues from the system's timing constraints, i.e. deadlines and rates. In fact, an upper bound on the length of the queue is provided by the maximum amount of data that can be produced during the maximum response time of the consumer [2]. On the other hand, since queues represent an additional cost to the system's implementation, we would be interested in finding a schedulable solution that minimizes the length of the required queues. This leads to a scheduling problem under precedence constraints in the more general form introduced in Section 3.

Indeed, let τ j be an event-driven task and τ i a lower priority data-flow task that receives inputs from τ j . As shown in Fig. 3, e i,j + 1 is an upper bound to the communication queue between τ j and τ i if
div.formula: a i (h) ≤ a j (k) ⇒ τ i (h) ≺ τ j (k + e i,j
div.p: ), because in such a case τ j cannot write more than e i,j + 1 times in the queue before τ i (h) completes. By considering e i,j a variable we will be able to define an optimization problem that minimizes the length of the communication queues, while preserving the system's schedulability.

Uniprocessor implementations of embedded controllers: the design of any control algorithm requires the verification of closed-loop stability. This is usually done by analyzing a mathematical model of the plant under control composed with the control algorithm. The result of this analysis provides the verification of stability in ideal conditions.
div.formula: i (h) ≤ a j (k) ⇒ τ i (h -1) ≺ τ j (k)
div.p: In the final implementation, the control algorithm is discretized and the computation of the control law takes a finite amount of time. In software implementations, different components of the system can be implemented as distinct tasks and these are executed asynchronously. Given the different model of computation, timing requirements are necessary to ensure that the system's stability is preserved. These requirements are of two kinds: computation latencies, to ensure that the result of the computation will be available when needed, and timing bounds on communication to ensure that data is not obsolete when it is used.

Computation latencies can be ensured in the implementation by using latencies as relative deadlines for the tasks. Bounds on communications can also be propagated as deadline constraints, forcing tasks to execute before data becomes obsolete. We see that the same mechanism, i.e. deadline assignment to tasks, is used for two different and possibly contrasting purposes.

The solution to this problem is obtained by modeling communication bounds as precedence constraints in the more general form provided by Def. 3.2. To see how the scheduling problem arises, let T i and T j be the inter-arrival times of τ i and τ j , respectively, and let B i,j be the maximum amount of time by which data produced by task τ i must be consumed by task τ j before it becomes obsolete. During the time interval B i,j we have at least as many as B i,j /T i different data produced by τ i . The communication bound requires that the consumer reads at least one of these data. This constraint can be modeled by the following precedence constraint:
div.formula: a i (h) ≤ a j (k) ⇒ τ i (h -d i,j ) ≺ τ j (k) where d i,j is subjected to the following condition: d i,j ≤ B i,j /T i . In Fig. 4, for example, d i,j = 1, which is acceptable if B i,j ≥ T i .

div.head: Scheduling under precedence constraints
div.p: Before introducing the general approach to scheduling under precedence constraints, we make an informal introduction to the basic ideas considering the special case of fixed priority scheduling. A simple way of enforcing the precedence constraint is by means of priority assignment: let τ i and τ j be two tasks and let τ i be assigned a higher priority than τ j , then if job τ i (h) is released before job τ j (k), τ i (h) will precede τ j (k). This is because τ j (k) cannot preempt τ i (h). Hence, more in general, for all non-negative integers d i,j and e i,j , τ i (hd i,j ) will precede τ j (k + e i,j ).

When τ i has not higher priority than τ j , the precedence constraint is not guaranteed unless timing conditions intervene to ensure the precedence relation between the two jobs. In particular, if the task's response time can be bounded, the completion of a given job cannot be deferred indefinetly in time. Hence, there will be some non-negative e i,j such that the precedence relation τ i (h) ≺ τ j (k + e i,j ) holds true due to the timing conditions. To see this let R i be an upper bound to the response time of τ i and let T j be a lower bound on the inter-arrival time of τ j , then there exists a positive integer e i,j such that R i ≤ e i,j T j . Hence, ∀e i,j ≥ Ri Tj , the precedence relation τ i (h) ≺ τ j (k + e i,j ) is guaranteed to hold true by the timing conditions of the schedule. Similarly, if T i is a lower bound on the inter-arrival time of τ i , there exists a positive integer
div.formula: d i,j such that R i ≤ d i,j T i . Hence, ∀d i,j ≥ Ri Ti , τ i (h -d i,j ) ≺ τ j (k).

Such a condition must be true for all non-negative integer values of d i,j and e i,j , if τ i has higher priority than τ j , while otherwise it must provide the timing condition given by Eq. 1: let p i,j be binary quantities representing the priority relation, i.e. p i,j = 1 if τ i has higher priority than τ j , while p i,j = 0 otherwise. If τ i does not have higher priority than τ j , then p i,j = 0 and Eq. 2 becomes d i,j T i + e i,j T j -R i ≥ 0, providing the timing condition given in Eq. 1.
In the next sections we generalize these ideas, providing general results and showing how these can be applied to specific scheduling policies.

div.head: Consistent scheduling with priorities
div.p: Most scheduling policies compute the schedule by assigning priorities to tasks and jobs. Priorities may be statically fixed (fixed priority scheduling) or dynamically computed (e.g. EDF scheduling). Let P i (h, t) denote the priority of job τ i (h) at time t. Although scheduling algorithms work on specific priority values, any schedule they produce only depends on the relative order of priorities. Hence, scheduling algorithms may be abstracted in terms of a priority relation between jobs.

div.head: Def. 5.1 We say that job τ i (h) has higher priority than job
div.formula: τ j (k), denoted by τ i (h) ≺ P τ j (k), if P i (h, t) > P j (k, t), ∀t such that max[r i (h), r j (k)] ≤ t < min[f i (h), f j (k)].
div.p: The order relation ≺ P is called the priority relation. The restriction of t to the interval between max[r i (h), r j (k)] and min[f i (h), f j (k)] is required, because in general only in this interval the priorities of τ i (h) and τ j (k) both have a meaning for the scheduling algorithm.

In scheduling with priorities, when a job τ i (h) has higher priority than a job τ j (k), τ j (k) cannot preempt τ i (h), i.e. either τ j (k) starts before the release of τ i (h) or τ j (k) starts after τ i (h) has finished. This is formalized by the following definition.

div.head: Def. 5.2 A schedule is said to satisfy a given priority relation if τ
div.formula: i (h) ≺ P τ j (k) ⇒ τ i (h) ≺ τ j (k) or r i (h) > s j (k).
div.p: Observe that the priority relation defines a precedence relation between jobs, hence, as discussed in Section 1, priorities can be effectively exploited to enforce precedence constraints. Indeed, when τ i (hd i,j ) has higher priority than τ j (k + e i,j ), it is sufficient that r i (hd i,j ) ≤ s j (k + e i,j ) to ensure the precedence relation, because τ j (k + e i,j ) cannot preempt τ i (hd i,j ). This condition is also necessary because s j (k + e i,j ) < r i (hd i,j ) implies that τ i (hd i,j ) cannot precede τ j (k + e i,j ). Nonetheless, it is not necessarily needed that τ i (hd i,j ) have higher priority than τ j (k + e i,j ), because timing conditions, as given in Theorem 5.1, may be sufficient to ensure the precedence relation. These facts are formalized in Theorem 5.2 below.

div.head: Application to specific scheduling policies
div.p: In the next sections we show the wide applicability of Theorem 5.2 by deriving sufficient conditions for scheduling under precedence constraints with FP and EDF. Similar results have been obtained for LLF as well, but will be omitted due to space limitations.

div.head: Consistent scheduling with fixed priorities
div.p: In this section we derive a sufficient condition for fixed priority scheduling under precedence constraints from the general condition expressed by Theorem 5.2.

Since priorities are fixed for every task, then P i (h, t) = P i , ∀h and ∀t. As shown in Section 5.2, we are interested in the priority relation, which can be represented by binary variables p i,j (h, k). In the case of fixed priorities these variables are independent of h and k and will be simply denoted by p i,j .
We assume that the inter-release time of every task can be lower-bounded, i.e. for all tasks τ i , there exist a constant T i such that T i ≤ T i (h, h + 1), ∀h.

It is well-known [12] that with fixed priority scheduling, if the inter-arrival time is lower-bounded, the response time can be upper-bounded, i.e. there exist constants R i such that R i (h) ≤ R i , ∀h.

Similarly, let I j be a lower bound on the idle time of task τ j , i.e. I j ≤ I j (k), ∀k, and let O i,j denote a lower bound on the offset of τ j with respect to τ i , when a i (h) ≤ a j (k), i.e. O i,j ≤ O i,j (h, k), ∀h, k such that a i (h) ≤ a j (k). div.head: Consistent scheduling with EDF
div.p: In this section we provide sufficient conditions for scheduling under precedence constraints when the EDF policy is used.
Let D i denote the relative deadline of task τ i , so that the absolute deadline of job τ i (h) is given by d i (h) = r i (h) + D i . By the EDF scheduling policy,
div.formula: P i (h, t) > P j (k, t) ⇔ d i (h) < d j (k).
div.p: Let T i , T j , I j and O i,j be bounds as introduced in Section 6.1. The following lemma provides the condition under which the job τ i (hd) has higher priority than the job τ j (k + e), when the EDF scheduling policy is used.

In [13], the authors show that EDF schedules satisfy precedence constraints if these are "consistent" with the release times and deadlines of the tasks, which in our notation can be expressed as G i,j = 1 ⇒ D i < D j and r i (k) ≤ r j (k), for all k. In [13], τ i and τ j are assumed to have the same period, i.e. a i (k) = a j (k), for all k, This result can be derived as a special case of Theorem 6.2. Corollary 6.2 Any schedule produced by EDF is consistent with a given precedence graph where d i,j = e i,j = 0, if a i (k) = a j (k), for all k, and G i,j = 1 ⇒ D i < D j and r i (k) ≤ r j (k).

Proof: Since the idle time is always non-negative by definition, I j = 0 can always be taken as its lower bound and the condition in Theorem 6.2 becomes: G i,j = 1 ⇒ D i < D j + O i,j and O i,j ≥ 0. We show now that this condition is implied by the condition in the corollary. Observe that r i (k) ≤ r j (k) implies r i (h) ≤ r j (k), for all h ≤ k, which in turn implies O i,j (h, k) ≥ 0, because O i,j (h, k) = r j (k)r i (h) by definition (see Fig. 5). Since a i (k) = a j (k), for all k, then a i (h) ≤ a j (k) implies h ≤ k. Therefore, 0 can be taken as a lower bound on the offset, i.e. O i,j ≥ 0. Moreover,
div.formula: D i < D j and O i,j ≥ 0 ⇒ D i < D j + O i,j . Hence, D i < D j and r i (k) ≤ r j (k) ⇒ D i < D j + O i,j
div.p: and O i,j ≥ 0, and the thesis follows.

div.head: Optimum priority/deadline assignment under precedence and schedulability constraints
div.p: In Section 5 we have developed the conditions for consistency with a given precedence graph. These conditions may impose constraints on the priorities assignment, for fixed priority scheduling, or may require to reduce task deadlines, for scheduling with EDF. This may cause the system to result unschedulable. With fixed processing resources, schedulability may be recovered by introducing non-negative integers d i,j and e i,j in the precedence constraints, as discussed in Section 3. In this respects, d i,j and e i,j represent a "relaxation" of the precedence constraints. We have shown in Section 4 that in most applications the constraint relaxation comes at a cost. For example in the case of mixed data-flow/event-driven real-time systems, higher relaxation requires longer buffers, while in the case of embedded controller, higher relaxation causes in general lesser margin for system's stability.

The above discussion suggests the definition of the following optimization problems: Fixed priority scheduling with given priorities: find the minimum relaxation of the precedence constraints (minimum non-negative values for d i,j and e i,j ) such that the system is schedulable;
Fixed priority scheduling with priority assignment: find the priority assignment such that the system is schedulable with minimum relaxation of the precedence constraints;
EDF scheduling: find the deadline assignment such that the original deadlines are satisfied and the system is schedulable with minimum relaxation of the precedence constraints.

div.head: Fixed priority scheduling with given priorities
div.p: The condition for consistency with a given precedence graph is given in Theorem 6.1. This condition requires the computation of the task's response time. If we consider the priorities as given, R i can be computed off-line by a well-known iterative formula [12]. Moreover, since the priorities are fixed, the schedulability condition may also be checked off-line. Any schedulability test presented in the literature [1,3,4,12] can be chosen. Hence, the optimization problem consists in finding the minimum values for d i,j and e i,j such that all precedence constraints are satisfied, leading to the following mathematical problem:
div.formula: MIN i,j G i,j (α i,j d i,j + β i,j e i,j ) 0 ≤ G i,j [d i,j T i -(1 -p i,j )R i + O i,j + e i,j T j + I j ]
div.p: where α i,j and β i,j are constant weight coefficients, that depend on the specific application case. The quantities d i,j and e i,j may be subjected to additional constraints, according to the given application at hand, which must be included in the problem. For example, in Section 4 a constraint of the form d i,j ≤ B i,j /T i was required.

div.head: Fixed priority scheduling with priority assignment
div.p: In the previous section, the optimization problem has been defined by considering the priorities as given, in which case the schedulability condition does not depend on the constraint relaxation. Here, we extend the problem by introducing priority assignment in the mathematical formulation. This will allow in general to reduce the global solution cost.

In [9] the authors formulate the priority assignment problem as a mathematical programming problem and show that it can be reduced to bilinear integer programming. As in [9], we represent the priority relation as a set of binary variables p i,j , as introduced in Section 6.1, and we need constraints for guaranteeing that they define a transitive non-symmetric relation. Observe that in general the priority relation is neither symmetric nor anti-symmetric, because tasks τ i and τ j may have the same priority, in which case p i,j = p j,i = 0. By the transitive property we must have that p i,j = p j,k = 1 ⇒ p i,k = 1, while non-symmetry requires that p i,j = 1 ⇒ p j,i = 0, which also implies p i,i = 0. These requirements can be formalized by the following constraints (see also [9]).
div.formula: p i,j + p j,i ≤ 1 (4) p i,j + p j,k -p i,k ≤ 1 (5)
div.p: When no pair of tasks have equal priority, the tasks's worst case response time is given by the formula [12]:
div.formula: R i = C i + k<i R i T k C k ,
div.p: where C i is the computing time of task τ i and the tasks are ordered by decreasing priority. As shown in [9], the re-sponse time computation can be expressed in terms of the priority relation:
div.formula: R i = C i + k p k,i R i T k C k
div.p: Note that two tasks τ i and τ k have equal priorities if and only if p i,k + p k,i = 0. Since Eq. 4 ensures that p i,k + p k,i evaluates to either 0 or 1, then τ i and τ j have equal priorities if and only if 1p i,kp k,i = 1. Hence, the response time computation can be extended to include tasks with equal priority as follows.
div.formula: R i = k (1 -p i,k -p k,i )C k + k p k,i R i T k C k (6)
div.p: Since the priority relation is variable we also need to include the schedulability condition as a constraint in our mathematical formulation. For fixed priority scheduling a general and precise schedulability test is represented by the condition R i ≤ D i , where D i is the relative deadline of task τ i .
The resulting mathematical problem providing the optimum priority assignment under precedence and schedulability constraints is shown below:
div.formula: MIN i,j G i,j (α i,j d i,j + β i,j e i,j ) 0 ≤ G i,j [d i,j T i -(1 -p i,j )R i + O i,j + e i,j T j + I j ] p i,j + p j,i ≤ 1 p i,j + p j,k -p i,k ≤ 1 R i = k [(1 -p i,k -p k,i )C k + p k,i Ri T k C k ] R i ≤ D i
div.p: As discussed in Section 7.1, specific constraints on the variables d i,j and e i,j may be included in the problem according to the given application at hand.

div.head: EDF scheduling
div.p: In this section we define the optimization problem arising when the EDF scheduling policy is used. Theorem 6.2 provides the conditions for consistency with a given precedence graph, so that the optimization problem can be defined as follows:
div.formula: MIN i,j G i,j (α i,j d i,j + β i,j e i,j ) 0 ≤ G i,j [D j -D i + d i,j T i + O i,j + e i,j T j ] 0 ≤ G i,j [d i,j T i + O i,j + e i,j T j + I j ]
div.p: In this problem, the schedulability condition can be checked off-line, because the relative deadlines are constant. Any schedulability test given in the literature [5,12,10] can be used to this purpose. We can extend this formulation introducing deadline assignment in the mathematical problem. To do so we must introduce an additional variable term in the relative deadline of each task. The new relative deadline of task τ i is then given by D ib i . The integer variables b i must be non-negative in order to guarantee that the original deadlines are met, while is an arbitrarily small positive constant. An upper bound to b i is provided by the fact that the relative deadline has not to be smaller than the task's computing time, i.e.
div.formula: C i ≤ D i -b i ⇔ b i ≤ Di-Ci .
div.p: Since changing the deadlines affects the schedulability condition, we need to introduce schedulability constraints in the problem. A precise schedulability test for EDF can be expressed as follows [5]:
div.formula: j L+Tj -Dj Tj C j ≤ L ∀L ∈ {d i (h)|d i (h) < L ub },
div.p: where d i (h) is the absolute deadline of job τ i (h) and L ub is an upper bound on L (see [5] for details).
The absolute deadline can be written as d i (h) = hT i + D i . Therefore, the set {d i (h)|d i (h) < L ub } can be expressed in the worst case as
div.formula: {hT i + D i | 0 ≤ h < (L ub -D i )/T i }.
div.p: Therefore, the schedulability test can be written as a set of constraints, one for each task, in the following form:
div.formula: j hTi+Di+Tj -Dj Tj C j ≤ hT i + D i (7) 0 ≤ h ≤ L ub -Di

div.p: To use the above schedulability condition we need to introduce the modified relative deadlines, D ib i . The resulting global optimization problem is shown below:
div.formula: MIN i,j G i,j (α i,j d i,j + β i,j e i,j ) 0 ≤ G i,j [D j -D i + (b i -b j ) + d i,j T i + O i,j + e i,j T j ] 0 ≤ G i,j [d i,j T i + O i,j + e i,j T j + I j ] 0 ≤ b i ≤ D i -C i j hTi+Di-bi +Tj -Dj +bj Tj C j ≤ hT i + D i -b i 0 ≤ h ≤ L ub -Di

div.head: Ti
div.p: Again, as discussed in Section 7.1, specific constraints on the variables d i,j and e i,j may be included in the problem according to the specific application at hand.

div.head: ILP formulation
div.p: The mathematical formulations of the optimization problems introduced in Section 7 contain non-linear functions, such as the ceiling and flooring functions and the product of variables, and are therefore computationally hard. The non-linear functions only appear in the computation of the task response time (Eq. 6) and in the schedulability condition for the EDF scheduling policy (Eq. 7). In this section we show that these problems can be reduced to corresponding integer linear programming (ILP) formulations.

In the response time computation the ceiling of the quantity R i /T k appears. The ceiling function can be removed by introducing additional integer variables, r i,k , subjected to the constraint 0 ≤ r i,k -R i /T k < 1, so that the response time computation can be formulated as
div.formula: R i = k (1 -p i,k -p k,i )C k + k p k,i r i,k C k = k (1 -p i,k -p k,i + p k,i r i,k )C k .
div.p: The respose time computation can now be linearized by removing the products p k,i r i,k . To this purpose we use the following lemma. Lemma 8.1 Let x be a variable with bounds V m ≤ x ≤ V M and let y be a binary variable, the product of x and y is given by z subjected to the following linear constraints:
div.formula: x -V M (1 -y) ≤ z ≤ x -V m (1 -y) (8) V m y ≤ z ≤ V M y(9)
div.p: Proof: When y = 1, Eq. 8 becomes x ≤ z ≤ x, hence z = x, while Eq. 9 gives V m ≤ z ≤ V M , which substituting the previous result provides the bounding conditions V m ≤ x ≤ V M , that hold true by hypothesis. When y = 0, Eq. 9 becomes 0 ≤ z ≤ 0, hence z = 0, while Eq. 8 provides
x-V M ≤ 0 and 0 ≤ x-V m , i.e. x ≤ V M and V m ≤ x, that are the bounding conditions, holding true by hypothesis. In conclusion, y = 1 ⇒ z = x, while y = 0 ⇒ z = 0. Since y is binary, then z = xy.

To apply Lemma 8.1, note that p k,i are binary variables and r i,k are bounded integer variables, because the schedulability condition requires that R i ≤ D i , so that r i,k = R i /T k ≤ D i /T k . Moreover, R i is lower-bounded by the task computing time C i , implying that C i /T k ≤ r i,k . Hence, to linearize the response time computation, Lemma 8.1 requires to introduce additional integer variables z i,k , representing the product p k,i r i,k , subjected to the following constraints:
div.formula: r i,k -Di T k (1 -p k,i ) ≤ z i,k ≤ r i,k -Ci T k (1 -p k,i ) p k,i Ci T k ≤ z i,k ≤ p k,i Di T k
div.p: The response time computation is then expressed by the following linear form:
div.formula: R i = k (1 -p i,k -p k,i + z i,k )C k . (10

div.head: Conclusions and future works
div.p: We have presented a novel approach to the problem of scheduling under precedence constraints, providing the general necessary and sufficient condition and formally discussing how this condition can be modified to keep the scheduling algorithm into account. We have shown how these general theorems can be applied in practice, when well-known scheduling policies are used, namely FP and EDF, and that several practical problems can be formalized using the more general definition proposed in this paper.

Moreover, we have shown that the developed theory can be successfully used to define a mathematical problem for allocating priorities (FP) or deadlines (EDF) in an optimum way under precedence and schedulability constraints. This problem has interesting applications to mixed dataflow/event-driven real-time systems and to the implementation of embedded controllers.

Future work include the extension of the theory and methods to multiprocessor, where tasks may run in parallel on different resources and communication delays between tasks allocated to different processing units may be non-negligible.
